title: A spectrum you could observe
blurb: From which lines I say exist to what a telescope would actually record.

steps.title: Which lines are strong
body: Selection rules say which transitions happen. My dipole engine says how fast, and I scale the bars by the spontaneous emission rate.
That is a rate, not a brightness. I have said nothing yet about how many atoms are in the upper level.

steps.title: How many atoms are actually there
body: Boltzmann populates the levels, Saha decides how much of the gas is still neutral, and now my bars mean emission rather than capability.
Move the temperature and I will make lines appear and vanish. Above about twenty thousand kelvin almost nothing is neutral, so every line I draw fades however hot it gets.

steps.title: What shape is a line
body: A line is not a spike. The upper level's finite lifetime gives Lorentzian wings, thermal motion gives a Gaussian core, and the real profile is their convolution.
I cannot show you this on the full-range axis, where a line is a fraction of a pixel wide. Click one and I will plot it linearly, at its actual shape.

steps.title: When a line stops measuring anything
body: Put more gas in the way and a weak line grows in proportion. A strong one does not: once its core is black it cannot absorb more, and a hundred times the gas barely widens it.

Tick the ringed box and I will plot that. The curve of growth is a state of this view rather than a state I hold, so I cannot switch it on for you here and I will not pretend the picture above already shows it. Its middle branch is where a line stops being a measurement of how much gas there is.

steps.title: Put the gas in front of a star
body: Now I put the same atoms between you and a continuum. I let each line absorb using only the atoms in its own lower level, which is why the Lyman lines go black while the Balmer lines are invisible in the very same gas.
That is the thing an emission spectrum cannot tell you, and it is why absorption spectroscopy is how we know what stars are made of.
